n: Lower Motor Neurone Lesions in Children

faq.a: The facial nerve nucleus supplies both upper and lower face; an LMN lesion interrupts the whole branch, so the forehead muscles are weak.
faq.q: Why is the forehead involved in a lower motor neurone facial palsy?

faq.a: If vital capacity falls below 15 mL/kg or there is bulbar weakness, ventilatory support is mandatory.
faq.q: Can a child with Guillain‑Barré survive without ventilation?

faq.a: Steroids help only in inflammatory facial palsy (Bell palsy); they are not beneficial in Guillain‑Barré or peripheral neuropathies.
faq.q: Is corticosteroid therapy useful for all LMN lesions?

exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with sudden unilateral facial weakness including the forehead after a recent measles infection – what is the most likely diagnosis and first‑line treatment? — Bell palsy; give oral steroids within 72 h and protect the eye.

A child with sickle‑cell disease develops progressive leg weakness and areflexia over 3 days; what urgent investigations and management steps are required? — Perform bedside neuro‑exam, consider Guillain‑Barré; obtain CSF if possible, start IVIG or plasma exchange, monitor respiratory function.

A 10‑year‑old with a history of a fall now has saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention and absent ankle reflexes – what lesion is most likely and how do you manage it? — Cauda equina syndrome from lumbosacral root compression; arrange urgent MRI (or treat presumptively) and surgical decompression.

Why should you avoid high‑dose steroids in an HIV‑positive child with peripheral neuropathy? — Steroids worsen immunosuppression and may precipitate opportunistic infections; treat underlying HIV and use neuropathic pain agents instead.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area presents with ascending weakness after a recent febrile illness; nerve conduction studies are unavailable – how do you confirm Guillain‑Barré? — Rely on clinical criteria (progressive symmetric weakness, areflexia, cranial nerve involvement) and CSF protein elevation if lumbar puncture is feasible.

Explain how you would differentiate a lower motor neurone facial palsy from a central facial palsy at the bedside. — Test forehead movement; LMN palsy shows inability to raise eyebrow, UMN palsy spares the forehead.

What are the key components of physiotherapy for a child with chronic LMN leg weakness? — Stretching to prevent contractures, strengthening of antagonist muscles, gait training with orthotics, and regular functional assessments.

In a resource‑limited setting, a child with suspected TB radiculitis cannot get MRI – what empirical treatment do you start and why? — Start standard anti‑TB therapy for 6 months because TB is common and untreated radiculitis can cause permanent paralysis.
ai.title: Lower Motor Neurone Lesions in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Lower motor neurone (LMN) lesions cause weakness, atrophy and reduced reflexes. Recognising patterns, common tropical causes and limited investigations guides urgent and long‑term care in low‑resource settings.

b: Flaccid weakness with decreased tone
Muscle atrophy over weeks
Fasciculations on inspection
Absent or markedly reduced deep tendon reflexes
sections.p: An LMN lesion is damage to the anterior horn cell, motor root, peripheral nerve or neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations and hyporeflexia.

b: MRC 5 = normal, 0 = no movement
Stage 1: mild weakness (MRC 4‑5), no atrophy
Stage 2: moderate weakness (MRC 3‑4), early atrophy
Stage 3: severe weakness (MRC 0‑2), marked atrophy
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impact (e.g., Medical Research Council (MRC) scale) and by the extent of muscle loss.

b: Post‑viral facial palsy (Bell palsy) – most common isolated LMN facial palsy
Guillain‑Barré syndrome (post‑diarrhoeal or post‑malaria)
Poliomyelitis (where still endemic)
Traumatic nerve root injury (e.g., L1‑L2 fracture)
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive neuropathy
HIV‑associated peripheral neuropathy
Tuberculous radiculitis (spinal TB)
Hereditary motor‑sensory neuropathy (Charcot‑Marie‑Tooth)
Herbal neurotoxins (e.g., cassava cyanide exposure)
sections.p: In East African children the commonest LMN aetiologies are infectious or post‑infectious, followed by trauma and hereditary neuropathies.

b: Facial LMN: inability to raise eyebrow, incomplete eye closure
Upper limb LMN: wrist drop, hand weakness, absent biceps reflex
Lower limb LMN: foot drop, absent ankle reflex, gait instability
Cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, areflexic anal tone
sections.p: Presentation varies with the level of the lesion; facial LMN palsy shows forehead involvement, limb LMN lesions give flaccid paresis, and root lesions may cause a saddle anaesthesia with bladder dysfunction.

t.b: Confirms pattern of weakness, tone, reflexes and fasciculations; distinguishes LMN from UMN lesions
Answers whether the lesion is demyelinating vs axonal; normal study suggests a neuromuscular junction problem
Detects albuminocytologic dissociation in Guillain‑Barré; if unavailable, rely on clinical progression and antecedent infection

t.a: Serology for HIV, hepatitis B, malaria rapid test
t.b: Identifies treatable infectious triggers; a positive result directs specific therapy
Shows compressive lesions such as TB abscess or disc herniation; if unavailable, treat presumptively based on clinical cauda equina signs

b: Progressive weakness >4 hours (risk of respiratory failure)
New onset dysphagia or facial bulbar weakness
Urinary retention or loss of anal tone
Severe autonomic instability (tachycardia, blood pressure swings)
sections.p: Prompt recognition of rapid progression, respiratory muscle involvement or autonomic failure prevents death.

b: Bell palsy – oral corticosteroids within 72 h; eye protection with lubricants and taping
Guillain‑Barré – IVIG (if available) or plasma exchange; monitor respiratory function
Poliomyelitis – supportive ventilation, physiotherapy, prevent secondary infections
TB radiculitis – standard anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 6 months
HIV neuropathy – optimise antiretroviral therapy; gabapentin for pain (avoid high‑dose steroids)
Trauma – surgical decompression if compressive fracture, immobilisation, analgesia
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and rehabilitation.

b: Monthly physiotherapy for the first 3 months, then quarterly
Assess gait and orthotics need in growing children
Vaccinate against polio, measles and varicella to reduce post‑viral LMN palsies
Screen HIV‑positive children for neuropathy annually
sections.p: Regular physiotherapy, monitoring for contractures and growth‑related functional loss are essential.

b: UMN lesion – spastic tone, hyperreflexia, forehead spared in facial palsy
Myasthenia gravis – fatigable weakness, normal tone, normal reflexes
Central facial palsy – forehead spared, contralateral lower face weakness
sections.p: Upper motor neurone lesions, myasthenia gravis and central facial palsy.

b: Early EMG may be normal; repeat after 1 week if suspicion persists
CSF protein may be normal in the first 3 days of Guillain‑Barré
sections.p: Normal reflexes early in Guillain‑Barré or early TB radiculitis may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening weakness or respiratory distress
New urinary retention or loss of anal tone
Severe facial swelling preventing eye closure
